tagline: Japan's classic onsen riviera — 3 million-plus overnight guests on a coast where every resort town faces the water and almost nothing moves by sea.
summary: The Izu Peninsula is Tokyo's weekend riviera: Atami's hot-spring high-rises, Itō's ryokan coast, Shimoda's historic harbour, and a UNESCO Global Geopark coastline wrapped around Suruga Bay — at 2,500 m, Japan's deepest bay, with Mt Fuji standing directly across the water. Atami alone logged a record 3.19 million overnight guests in FY2025. Yet the resort towns are linked almost entirely by congested coastal roads and trains; the sea in front of them is empty. A coastal foiling network turns the peninsula's geography — town-to-town hops of 5–25 nm and a ~50 nm run from Tokyo Bay — into its transport system, with the Fuji sightline as the signature ride.

demand_signals.label: Atami overnight guests
demand_signals.note: Atami Tourism Bureau reported FY2025 lodging guests surpassing the previous record; the town has fully recovered past pre-COVID levels and is supply-constrained on access.

demand_signals.label: UNESCO Global Geopark coast
demand_signals.note: The whole peninsula is a UNESCO Global Geopark; Suruga Bay plunges to ~2,500 m (Japan's deepest) and Sagami Bay to ~1,500 m — a dramatic, deep-water coastline made for low-wake, clean marine operations.

demand_signals.label: Road-bound resort access
demand_signals.value: One coastal rail line + chronically congested Route 135
demand_signals.note: Weekend traffic from Tokyo regularly doubles drive times to Itō and Shimoda; the train from Atami to Shimoda takes ~1h30 for ~24 nm of coast. The sea-side doors of every resort face an unused highway.

demand_signals.label: Adjacent foil-borne market
demand_signals.note: Tokyo's jetfoil-served island chain sits directly across the Sagami water from Atami/Itō — passengers in this region already ride hydrofoils, and the island and peninsula economies can be stitched into one network.

use_cases.title: Onsen-coast hopper (Atami ↔ Itō ↔ Shimoda)
use_cases.body: A scheduled foiling service down the east coast — Atami to Itō ~10 nm, Itō to Shimoda ~24 nm — replaces the congested coastal road with a 20–40 minute glide past the Geopark cliffs, delivering guests to resort jetties and harbours.

use_cases.title: Tokyo ↔ Atami premium arrival
use_cases.body: The ~50 nm run from Tokyo Bay to Atami is the marquee arrival: a smooth foil-borne alternative for the capital's weekend flow, with Quanta-LR adding all-weather hybrid capacity on the exposed cross-Sagami water.

use_cases.title: Mt Fuji sightline cruises on Suruga Bay
use_cases.body: Suruga Bay's west coast (Heda, Toi, Mito) faces Mt Fuji straight across Japan's deepest water — a near-silent foiling charter with the country's most iconic sightline, plus direct links to Shimizu on the far shore.

use_cases.title: Island cross-link
use_cases.body: Itō/Atami ↔ Izu Ōshima (~19–24 nm) joins the peninsula's onsen economy to Tokyo's volcanic island chain — two destination markets, one all-electric hop.

journeys.today: ~1h30 on the single-track coastal rail line or longer on the chronically jammed Route 135.
journeys.with_navier: A ~30 nm foiling run down the Geopark coast — under an hour, smooth, with the cliffs and Sagami Bay as the view.

journeys.today: Shinkansen plus local transfers, or 2–3 hours by car on a good day — the sea route doesn't exist.
journeys.with_navier: A ~50 nm foil-borne arrival straight to the onsen waterfront — the premium gateway for 3M+ annual overnight guests.

journeys.today: Limited seasonal sailings; most island traffic detours through central Tokyo.
journeys.with_navier: A ~20 nm all-electric cross-link to the volcano island — peninsula onsen and island caldera in one itinerary.

journeys.today: The Suruga Bay ferry crossing has been under repeated threat of discontinuation; otherwise it's a long drive around the bay head.
journeys.with_navier: A clean, fast crossing of Japan's deepest bay with Mt Fuji dead ahead — modernising a crossing locals have fought to keep alive.

navier_fit.pioneer_ii: The entire resort coast is an all-electric mesh: Atami ↔ Hatsushima ~6 nm, Atami ↔ Itō ~10 nm, Itō ↔ Shimoda ~24 nm, Suruga Bay crossings ~15–20 nm, and the Ōshima cross-links ~19–24 nm — every leg deep inside the 70 nm envelope, on a coast with strong grid access.
navier_fit.quanta_lr: Tokyo ↔ Atami (~50 nm) is in electric range but the exposed cross-Sagami water (winter swell 1.5–3.0 m) makes hybrid foiling stability valuable for all-weather schedule-keeping; Quanta-LR also extends service around the peninsula tip and onward to the outer Izu Islands (~85–155 nm) without any island charging dependency.

competitive_landscape: Water transport today is thin and fragmented: Tokai Kisen's jet ferries call at Atami/Itō seasonally en route to the islands, the small Suruga Bay ferry (Shimizu ↔ Toi) has repeatedly faced discontinuation, and Hatsushima island is served by a conventional shuttle — while the dominant flows move by the single-track Izukyū rail line and the congested Route 135. Millions of visitors a year to a coast-hugging resort chain with almost no coastal water service is the demand evidence: the corridor exists, the vehicles don't.

precedents.why_it_matters: The resort-coast playbook at national scale — phased, two-platform, first 5 vessels in 2026.

precedents.what: Four decades of jetfoil passenger service on adjacent water
precedents.why_it_matters: Foil-borne travel is a proven, adopted behaviour on this exact body of water.

seasonality: Typhoon season (Jun–Oct) and winter NW swell on the Sagami side define the exposure calendar; Suruga Bay's west coast is more sheltered. Foiling above the chop widens the operable window on the east-coast legs and makes the calm spring/autumn peaks — cherry blossom, autumn leaves, and Atami's year-round fireworks calendar — fully serviceable. Summer demand peaks align with the calmest inshore conditions outside typhoon passages.
regulatory_note: Pier and harbour jurisdiction sits with Shizuoka Prefecture (with Atami, Itō and Shimoda ports municipally operated), under MLIT Maritime Bureau and Japan Coast Guard certification. The UNESCO Global Geopark designation and Suruga Bay's deep-water ecology give clean, low-wake operations a concrete mandate, aligned with Japan's 2050 carbon-neutrality target and MLIT zero-emission-vessel programmes. Greenfield resort-pier upgrades at Shimoda and the west coast are open design-in opportunities.
